rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Noah narrative develops the question in 54:4: Quraysh should learn from earlier nations who rejected messengers and were punished, rather than follow their path toward doom.
rows.anchor: why they do not seek a lesson from the history of previous nations which has been narrated to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's Book is a graciously revealed, fully equipped means for educating and instructing Quraysh.
rows.anchor: This Book is fully equipped with everything needed to educate and remind them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah is placed first in the chronological survey; his rejection assures Muhammad that he is not the first messenger rejected, and Quraysh will share earlier rejecters' fate if they follow them.
rows.anchor: Since the sequence adopted is chronological, the anecdote of Noah (sws) is mentioned first

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed fa is explicative: after a brief reference to Noah's people's denial, it introduces the incident's details.
rows.anchor: is for explication. After briefly referring to the incident, with these words begin the details

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Noah God's servant expresses divine affection for him.
rows.anchor: The affection of God for Noah (sws) reflected in the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's people mistook worldly affluence and honor for proof of God's favor and future rank; annoyed by his persistent warnings, they called him mad to discredit him and reassure the masses.
rows.anchor: they would also try to assure the masses that they should not be influenced by the warnings of the messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase describes Noah's people's threat to stone him; 26:116 gives their warning that he would be stoned if he did not desist.
rows.anchor: If you do not desist from your ways, you shall end among those who have been stoned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After his people threatened to stone him, Noah says he has exhausted his power to convince them and asks God to deal with the arrogant people.
rows.anchor: he no longer had the power to continue, and hence God should then deal with these arrogant people in His own way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intiṣār means defending or taking revenge; Noah asks God to help him take revenge for their arrogance.
rows.anchor: means “to defend” and “to take revenge.” Noah (sws) requested God to help him take revenge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi points readers to Sūrah Nūḥ for the complete details of Noah's prayer.
rows.anchor: The complete details of Noah’s prayer are mentioned in Sūrah Nūḥ ahead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flood came after Noah's prayer: rain poured through the opened heavenly gates while springs burst from the earth, turning it into seas, rivers, and canals.
rows.anchor: The Almighty opened the gates of the sky with water pouring forth, and caused the earth to burst with gushing springs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waters met at the level God had fixed, engulfing Noah's people so that none could escape.
rows.anchor: the point up to which the Almighty had fixed for the water to rise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says he has already discussed the flood's details in his exegesis of Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt.
rows.anchor: I have already mentioned its details in the exegesis of Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ark's planks and nails, built under God's directive, highlight His power, wisdom, affection, mercy, and majesty: divine mercy could save Noah with logs, while without it even warships and dams fail.
rows.anchor: the real thing is God’s mercy and affection. If they are with a person, then a few logs can save them from Noah’s deluge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ark sailed safely under God's special protection; other people's boats could not help them because they lacked that protection.
rows.anchor: others too had their boats; however, these boats could not be of any benefit to them because they did not have God’s protection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about recompense refers to God's majestic aid for His servant who had been slighted, recalling Noah's plea that he was vanquished.
rows.anchor: the Almighty showed His majesty in order to help His servant who had been slighted and not duly honoured

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in the verse can refer to the land mentioned in 54:12 or to Noah's widely transmitted, well-known story.
rows.anchor: can be the land referred to earlier in verse twelve by the words

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some take the pronoun to refer to remains of Noah's Ark seen by later generations on Mount Jūdī; Islahi gives this view no weight.
rows.anchor: Some people regard the antecedent of this pronoun to be the remains of Noah’s Ark

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth and history offer abundant signs and lessons; what is scarce is a heart able to heed them.
rows.anchor: as far as signs and warning lessons are concerned, there are several on this earth and in history as well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nudhur is originally nudhurī; its yāʾ is dropped for rhyme, with the kasrah remaining.
rows.anchor: owing to the rhyme and the kasrah present as its remnant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nudhur is a noun derived from indhār and means warnings or admonition.
rows.anchor: it means “warnings” and “admonition.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anyone willing to listen and learn can see in Noah's story how severe God's punishment is and how precisely His warnings come to pass.
rows.anchor: if a person has ears to pay heed and a heart to learn a lesson, he can see in this anecdote how profound is God’s punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reminder verse recurs after each prophetic story, so Islahi says its explanation need not be repeated at every occurrence.
rows.anchor: This verse will be repeated after the end of every Prophetic anecdote

rows.speaker: people generally
rows.claim: People generally read the verse as saying the Qur'an is easy to memorize and consult for counsel; Islahi accepts this inference as correct but says the verse has wider scope.
rows.anchor: People have generally interpreted this verse to mean that the Almighty has made the Qur’ān a very easy book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taysīr means fitting something to its purpose and equipping it with the needed means; Islahi illustrates it as preparing a horse for riding and a person for a campaign.
rows.anchor: to make something appropriate for a specific objective and to embellish it with all the required means and needs

rows.speaker: Muḍarris ibn Rub‘ī
rows.claim: Muḍarris ibn Rub‘ī's cited poem describes helping a leader prepare for a campaign and equipping him to discharge leadership duties, witnessing this sense of taysīr.
rows.anchor: A poet, Muḍ arris ibn Rub‘ ī, belonging to the age of ignorance says

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr here covers educating, instructing, reminding, informing, warning, counseling, teaching a lesson, and conclusively communicating the truth.
rows.anchor: The meanings of educating and instructing the readers as well as reminding, informing, warning, counselling, teaching a lesson

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an does not impose alien knowledge; it revives innate treasures of knowledge and understanding that people neglect.
rows.anchor: does not impose something external on us; on the contrary, it revives and highlights the treasures of knowledge and cognizance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder verse follows the earlier statement that the punishment warned of by the Prophet is inevitable.
rows.anchor: Earlier in the sūrah, it was said that the punishment which the Prophet (sws) was warning them of was inevitable
